title: Extensions of polynomial modules preserve the good locus
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n\geq0$, and $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. For a $P$-module $N$, let $G_R(N)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] be the union of $D(f)=\{\mathfrak p:f\notin\mathfrak p\}$ over $f\in R$ such that $N_f$ is free over $R_f$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module] and finitely presented over $R_f[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ [def-sc-finitely-presented-module]. Here $R_f=R[1/f]$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away], $N_f$ is the localization of the underlying $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away], and the polynomial action is $x_i(m/f^a)=(x_im)/f^a$. Let $M_1\xrightarrow{u}M_2\xrightarrow{v}M_3$ be $P$-linear maps with $u$ injective, $v$ surjective, and $\operatorname{im}u=\ker v$. Then $$G_R(M_1)\cap G_R(M_3)\subseteq G_R(M_2).$$ Freeness here permits arbitrary, including infinite or empty, bases. No reducedness, finiteness, or nonzero-ring assumption is imposed.

source.place: Tag 051W (lemma-generic-flatness-locus-extension), specialized to the polynomial algebra; equations equation-flat-and-finitely-presented and equation-good-locus.

proof.text: Fix $\mathfrak p\in G_R(M_1)\cap G_R(M_3)$. By the definition of these unions choose $a,b\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ such that $(M_1)_a$ is free over $R_a$ and finitely presented over $R_a[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, and similarly $(M_3)_b$ over $R_b$. Put $f=ab$. Primality gives $f\notin\mathfrak p$. It remains to prove the two good conditions for $(M_2)_f$.

source.place: Tag 051W (lemma-generic-flatness-locus-extension), specialized to the polynomial algebra; equations equation-flat-and-finitely-presented and equation-good-locus.

proof.text: Use the fraction definition of module localization [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away]. For any $P$-module $N$ and $c,d\in R$, put $h=cd$. The identification $(N_c)_d\cong N_h$ sends $(m/c^i)/d^j$ to $c^{k-i}d^{k-j}m/h^k$, where $k\geq i,j$; the inverse sends $m/h^k$ to $(m/c^k)/d^k$. Changing $k$, or a representative fraction, leaves these classes unchanged by the defining equality after multiplication by a power of the denominator. Composing the two displayed formulas gives the original classes. The maps commute with addition, base scalars and each $x_i$ by the fraction formulas. For $N=R$ this identifies $(R_c)_d$ with $R_h$. For the polynomial algebra $R_c[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, localizing at the constant $d$ gives $(R_c)_d[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$: the map divides every coefficient by the same power of $d$; its inverse puts a finite list of coefficient denominators over a common power. The same formulas show that localization as a polynomial module agrees with localization of its underlying base module. Apply these identifications to $(c,d)=(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$.

source.place: Tag 00CS, proposition-localization-exact; Tag 051W, lemma-generic-flatness-locus-extension, passage to f=f_1f_3.

proof.text: The bases of $(M_1)_a$ over $R_a$ and $(M_3)_b$ over $R_b$ remain bases after the further localizations of step 2. Indeed, for a module $F$ with basis $(e_i)$ over a ring $A$, every $m/d^j\in F_d$ is the finite linear combination of $e_i/1$ obtained by dividing the coordinates of $m$ by $d^j$. A relation with finite support among $e_i/1$ can be put over a common power $d^j$; if it vanishes, a further power of $d$ kills the numerator in $F$, and the uniqueness of the original coordinates says that this power kills every coefficient. Thus each localized coefficient is zero. This proves existence and uniqueness of coordinates, including for an infinite or empty indexing set. Hence $(M_1)_f$ and $(M_3)_f$ are free over $R_f$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module].

source.place: Tag 051W (lemma-generic-flatness-locus-extension), specialized to the polynomial algebra; equations equation-flat-and-finitely-presented and equation-good-locus.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-localization-preserves-finite-presentation] to the commutative ring $A=R_a[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, the $A$-module $(M_1)_a$, and the multiplicative set of powers of the constant $b$. Step 2 identifies the resulting ring with $R_f[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and the resulting module with $(M_1)_f$. This proves finite presentation of $(M_1)_f$ over that ring. Interchange $a,b$ and use $(M_3)_b$ to prove the same for $(M_3)_f$. No finite presentation over the base $R_a$ or $R_b$ is asserted or needed.

source.place: Tag 00CS, proposition-localization-exact; Tag 051W, lemma-generic-flatness-locus-extension, passage to f=f_1f_3.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-p1-localization-short-exact] to the given short exact sequence, regarded as one of $R$-modules, and to the multiplicative set $\{f^j:j\geq0\}$. We obtain $0\to(M_1)_f\xrightarrow{u_f}(M_2)_f\xrightarrow{v_f}(M_3)_f\to0$. Here $u_f(m/f^j)=u(m)/f^j$ and likewise for $v_f$. These maps are also linear over $B=R_f[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$: they commute with localized scalars and with $x_i$ since $u,v$ were $P$-linear. Thus the same underlying exact sequence is short exact both over $R_f$ and over $B$.

source.place: Tag 00CS, proposition-localization-exact; Tag 051W, lemma-generic-flatness-locus-extension, passage to f=f_1f_3.

proof.text: Choose bases $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of $(M_1)_f$ and $(q_j)_{j\in J}$ of $(M_3)_f$ over $R_f$, and for each $j$ choose $t_j\in(M_2)_f$ with $v_f(t_j)=q_j$. The family $(u_f(e_i))_{i\in I}$ together with $(t_j)_{j\in J}$ is a basis: given $z$, subtract the finite combination of $t_j$ with coefficients the coordinates of $v_f(z)$, then use exactness to express the remainder in $u_f((M_1)_f)$. A finite relation among this family maps under $v_f$ to a relation among the $q_j$, whose coefficients vanish; injectivity of $u_f$ and independence of the $e_i$ kill all remaining coefficients. Thus $(M_2)_f$ is free over $R_f$ by [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. The construction uses only finite combinations even for infinite bases.

source.place: Tag 051W (lemma-generic-flatness-locus-extension), specialized to the polynomial algebra; equations equation-flat-and-finitely-presented and equation-good-locus.

proof.text: By step 5, $u_f$ identifies $(M_1)_f$ with the $B$-submodule $K=\ker(v_f)$ of $(M_2)_f$, so $K$ is finitely presented: compose a finite presentation of $(M_1)_f$ with this $B$-linear isomorphism. Step 4 also gives finite presentation of $(M_3)_f$, and $v_f$ is surjective. Apply [lem-trf-module-finite-presentation-of-kernel] with ring $B$, source $(M_2)_f$, target $(M_3)_f$, and map $v_f$. Its two finite-presentation hypotheses are exactly those just established. Hence $(M_2)_f$ is finitely presented over $B$.

source.place: Tag 0519, lemma-extension (2); Tag 051W, lemma-generic-flatness-locus-extension, last three sentences.

proof.text: Steps 6 and 7 show that $f$ is one of the elements defining $G_R(M_2)$. Since $\mathfrak p\in D(f)$ by step 1, it follows that $\mathfrak p\in G_R(M_2)$. This proves the required inclusion.
